content: Glycophorin A (GPA), also referred to as GYPA, is a protein encoded by the GYPA gene in humans. It has also been classified as CD235a (Cluster of Differentiation 235a). Function Glycophorins A (GYPA) and B (GYPB) are the primary sialoglycoproteins found in the human erythrocyte membrane. These proteins carry the antigenic determinants for the MN and Ss blood group systems. In addition to the common M, N, S, and s antigens, which are present across all populations, approximately 40 related variant phenotypes have been identified. These include variants of the Miltenberger complex, as well as isoforms such as Sta, Dantu, Sat, He, Mg, and deletion variants like Ena, S-s-U-, and Mk. Most of these variants arise from gene recombination events between GYPA and GYPB. Genomics The GYPA, GYPB, and GYPE genes belong to the same family and are located on the long arm of chromosome 4 (4q31). This gene family evolved through two distinct gene duplication events. The first duplication event led to the creation of two genes, one of which evolved into GYPA, while the other underwent a second duplication to form GYPB and GYPE. These events likely occurred within a relatively short evolutionary timeframe, with the second duplication resulting from an unequal crossing-over event. The GYPA gene itself consists of seven exons and shares 97% sequence homology with GYPB and GYPE from the 5' untranslated region (UTR) to the coding sequence for the first 45 amino acids. The exon at this point encodes the transmembrane domain. An Alu repeat is located within the intron downstream of this region, where the crossover event that created the ancestral genes for GYPA and GYPB/E occurred. GYPA is found in all primates, while GYPB is present only in gorillas and some higher primates, suggesting that the duplication events occurred relatively recently. Molecular Biology Each erythrocyte contains approximately one million copies of the Glycophorin A protein. Blood Groups The MN blood group system was the second set of antigens to be discovered. The M and N antigens were identified in 1927 by Landsteiner and Levine, while the S and s antigens were described later in 1947. The frequencies of these antigens vary among populations: M: 78% in Caucasians, 74% in individuals of African descent. N: 72% in Caucasians, 75% in individuals of African descent. S: 55% in Caucasians, 31% in individuals of African descent. s: 89% in Caucasians, 93% in individuals of African descent. Molecular Medicine Transfusion Medicine The M and N antigens differ at two amino acid residues. The M allele has serine at position 1 (C at nucleotide 2) and glycine at position 5 (G at nucleotide 14), while the N allele has leucine at position 1 (T at nucleotide 2) and glutamate at position 5 (A at nucleotide 14). Both Glycophorin A and B bind to the Vicia graminea anti-N lectin. Approximately 40 variants in the MN blood group system have been identified, primarily due to mutations within the 4 kb region coding for the extracellular domain. These include antigens such as Mg, Dantu, Henshaw (He), Miltenberger, Nya, Osa, Orriss (Or), Raddon (FR), and Stones (Sta). Chimpanzees also possess an MN blood antigen system, with M reacting strongly and N reacting weakly. Null Mutants Individuals lacking both Glycophorin A and B exhibit a phenotype designated as Mk. Dantu Antigen The Dantu antigen, first described in 1984, has an apparent molecular weight of 29 kDa and consists of 99 amino acids. The first 39 amino acids are derived from Glycophorin B, while residues 40–99 are derived from Glycophorin A. Dantu is associated with a very weak s antigen, a protease-resistant N antigen, and either a very weak or absent U antigen. At least three variants of Dantu (MD, NE, and Ph) have been identified. Henshaw Antigen The Henshaw (He) antigen results from a mutation in the N-terminal region, with three differences in the first five amino acid residues. The usual sequence is Tryptophan1-Serine-Threonine-Serine-Glycine5, while Henshaw has Leucine1-Serine-Threonine-Threonine-Glutamate5. This antigen is found in 1% of individuals of African origin in the US and UK and 7% of West Africans. At least three variants of this antigen have been identified. Miltenberger Subsystem The Miltenberger (Mi) subsystem originally consisted of five phenotypes (Mia, Vw, Mur, Hil, and Hut) but now includes 11 recognized phenotypes (Mi-I to Mi-XI). These phenotypes are based on reactions with standard antisera. Mi-I (Mia), Mi-II (Vw), Mi-VII, and Mi-VIII are carried on Glycophorin A. Mi-I results from a mutation at amino acid 28 (threonine to methionine: C → T at nucleotide 83), leading to the loss of glycosylation at the asparagine26 residue. Mi-II results from a mutation at amino acid 28 (threonine to lysine: C → A at nucleotide 83), also resulting in the loss of glycosylation at asparagine26. Mi-VII is due to a double mutation in Glycophorin A, converting arginine to threonine and tyrosine to serine at positions 49 and 52, respectively. Mi-VIII results from a mutation at amino acid residue 49 (arginine → threonine). Other Miltenberger variants arise from rearrangements of Glycophorin A and B. Stones Antigen The Stones (Sta) antigen is produced by a hybrid gene, with the 5' half derived from Glycophorin B and the 3' half from Glycophorin A. It is now considered part of the Miltenberger complex. Sat Antigen The Sat antigen gene contains six exons, with exons I–IV identical to the N allele of Glycophorin A, while exons V and VI are derived from Glycophorin B. The mature SAT protein contains 104 amino acids. Orriss Antigen The Orriss (Or) antigen appears to be a mutant of Glycophorin A, but its precise nature remains undetermined. Mg Antigen The Mg antigen is carried on Glycophorin A and lacks three O-glycosylated side chains. Os Antigen The Osa (MNS38) antigen results from a mutation at nucleotide 273 (C → T) within exon 3, replacing a proline residue with serine. Ny Antigen The Nya (MNS18) antigen results from a mutation at nucleotide 194 (T → A), substituting an aspartate residue with glutamate. Reactions Anti-M antibodies, though naturally occurring, are rarely implicated in transfusion reactions. Anti-N antibodies are not considered to cause transfusion reactions. Severe reactions have been reported with anti-Miltenberger antibodies. Anti-Mi-I (Vw) and Mi-III have been recognized as causes of hemolytic disease of the newborn. The Raddon antigen has been associated with severe transfusion reactions. Relevance for Infection The Wright b antigen (Wrb), located on Glycophorin A, serves as a receptor for the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum. Erythrocytes lacking Glycophorin A (Ena-) are resistant to invasion by this parasite. The erythrocyte binding antigen 175 of P. falciparum recognizes the terminal Neu5Ac(α2-3)Gal sequences of Glycophorin A. Several viruses, including hepatitis A virus, bovine parvovirus, Sendai virus, influenza A and B, group C rotavirus, encephalomyocarditis virus, and reoviruses, also bind to Glycophorin A.
